A rectory is a house — a real, ordinary house — that a church provides for its rector (a type of Christian priest or minister) to live in. Think of it as the official home that comes with the job of being a rector. The rector doesn't own it; the church does. It's provided so that the clergyman has a place to live right there, close to the church he serves.

To understand "rectory," you first need to understand "rector," because the word rectory literally means "the house of a rector."

A rector is a clergyman — a religious leader — who is placed in charge of a specific parish. A parish is a local church community: a specific church and all the people who belong to it in the surrounding area.

  • In the Anglican Church (Church of England, and its related churches like the Episcopal Church in the United States), a rector is the priest who is the permanent, head leader of a parish. He is responsible for the spiritual care of everyone in that parish — conducting services, performing baptisms, weddings, funerals, visiting the sick, and so on.
  • In the Roman Catholic Church, a rector is a priest who heads a particular church, college, or seminary.
So What Exactly Is a Rectory?

A rectory is simply the house where this rector lives, provided to him by the church as part of his position.

Imagine you get a job as the head of a local fire station, and the station has a small apartment attached to it where the chief is expected to live. The rectory works similarly — it is the house attached to (or near) the rector's church, provided so the rector can be close to his work and community at all times.

It is not a religious building. You won't find pews, altars, or chapels inside a rectory (usually). It is a normal domestic home — with bedrooms, a kitchen, a living room — where the rector and often his family live their everyday lives.

The church owns the rectory. The rector merely lives in it for as long as he holds his position. When he moves on or retires, the next rector moves in.

A rectory is almost always right next to the church, or very close to it. This is intentional. The rector needs to be available to his parishioners at all times — for emergencies, for counseling, for prayer. Having him live right beside the church makes this possible.

If you've ever walked past an old church in England or Ireland and noticed a larger house sitting beside or behind it, that house is very likely the rectory. In fact, in many English villages, the church and the rectory sitting side by side is one of the most iconic, recognizable sights.

Historically, rectories could be quite large and grand — sometimes even grand manor houses. This is because, in older times in England, a rector had legal rights to collect income from the land of his parish (called tithes), which sometimes made the position quite wealthy. A wealthy rector meant a wealthy rectory.

In modern times, rectories are generally more modest — comfortable family homes, but nothing extravagant. Many older, larger rectories have been sold off by churches over the years, as maintaining big houses became expensive.

English has several words for "a house provided to a clergyman," and they can be confusing. Here's how to keep them apart:

  • Rectory → the house of a rector (Anglican or Catholic)
  • Vicarage → the house of a vicar (another type of Anglican clergyman, slightly different role from a rector)
  • Parsonage → a general, broad term for any house provided to any type of Christian minister or pastor; it's the umbrella word
  • Manse → the house of a minister in Presbyterian or other Protestant traditions
  • Palace → used for a bishop's official residence (bishops being senior to rectors)

So rectory is a specific type of parsonage. All rectories are parsonages, but not all parsonages are rectories.

Imagine a small English village in the 1800s. In the center sits a stone church with a tall steeple. Right beside it, separated only by a garden wall, is a two-storey brick house with ivy climbing its walls. That house is the rectory. Inside lives Reverend Clarke, the rector of this parish, along with his wife and children. He walks from the rectory to the church every morning. When a parishioner is in distress in the middle of the night, they knock on the rectory door. When the church needs to be unlocked on a weekday morning, he steps out of the rectory and does it himself.

That is the rectory — not just a house, but the lived-in heart of a parish, right beside its church.

What it isA house provided by a church for its rector to live in
Who lives thereThe rector (a Christian clergyman in charge of a parish)
Who owns itThe church (not the rector personally)
Where it's foundNext to or very near the church it belongs to
What it looks likeAn ordinary house — historically sometimes large and grand, today typically a modest family home
Broader categoryIt is a type of parsonage (the general word for any clergyman's official home)

The word "rectory" in everyday use almost always refers to this physical house. If you read it in a novel, a news article, or a historical account, picture a house standing beside a church — and you'll have it exactly right.
